segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, here's something that happens all summer long on Highway 101 in Northern California in the middle of the redwood forest. Little kids hold conversations with a statue that's five stories high.

segments.speaker: Child
segments.text: What do you eat?

segments.speaker: Paul Bunyan Statue
segments.text: What do I eat? Mostly pancakes.

segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.text: What do you eat?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The statue is Paul Bunyan. Big red shirt, blue pants, hairy chest, black beard. He stands next to Babe, his 36-foot tall blue ox. Adults talk to him too.

segments.speaker: Man 1

segments.speaker: Paul Bunyan Statue
segments.text: Yeah, I play poker with him on Friday nights.

segments.text: Uh.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Paul and Babe are part of a roadside attraction called Trees of Mystery. Paul can turn his head in a slow swivel. He can wave. He can wink. All with the stiff, hydraulic-powered gestures you would expect from a statute built in 1962, which he is.

segments.speaker: Morgan Gossage
segments.text: Can I sing you a song?

segments.text: Can you sing me a song?

segments.text: OK. [SINGS]

segments.speaker: Paul Bunyan Statue
segments.text: This is a good one.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Eight year-old Morgan Gossage, like lots of kids, also has skeptical questions for Paul Bunyan. So many kids try to trap him into admitting he is not really Paul Bunyan, he's just a statue.

segments.speaker: Morgan Gossage
segments.text: Why can't you open your mouth when you talk?

segments.text: Oh, I can. I don't need to, though.

segments.speaker: Morgan Gossage
segments.text: Huh.

segments.speaker: Paul Bunyan Statue
segments.text: I can't dance. I can't jump up and down.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Management, by the way, holds the line on this. When one of our producers first spoke with a woman in the gift shop and asked who does the voice for Paul Bunyan, the woman replied, "Paul Bunyan."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Or this is John Thompson. His family owns Trees of Mystery and he runs the place. I asked him what Paul's made of. He says, "The same stuff as you or I, only more of it." I ask if Paul Bunyan's an employee.

segments.speaker: John Thompson
segments.text: Well, you know, there's that fuzzy area there because he's so big we can't really get him to do what we want him to do all the time. It's only been a few years we got him to stop walking around in the daytime. He stepped on a couple cars and made a mess. But that's Paul.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: John's daughter Hannah and his son-in-law Kylan both listened to him tell me this. They both seemed a little pained to have to keep up the pretense with me that Paul was real. And it's Kylan who pipes in with a very reasonable point that if Paul Bunyan is just some guy pretending to be Paul Bunyan--

segments.speaker: Kylan
segments.text: You know, it really isn't as fun. I don't think the truth is really as interesting as people want to believe it is. It really isn't, you know?

segments.speaker: John Thompson
segments.text: The bottom line, Ira, is that would you pull the mask off Mickey Mouse?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Me? No.

segments.speaker: John Thompson
segments.text: Well, there you go.

segments.speaker: Kylan
segments.text: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: John Thompson
segments.text: OK?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK. And I'll be frank, I thought this is where the story would end. We have an episode for you today about secret identities.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And at this point, I would say something about how it's better not to find out who's behind the mask and I would start the show WBEZ Chicago, Public Radio International, all that blah, blah, blah. And we would move on to Act One.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But around closing time at Trees of Mystery, that plan fell completely apart. I was standing near Paul Bunyan and this heavyset guy in a t-shirt and jeans and wire-rimmed glasses walked up to me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Hi. Ira.

segments.speaker: Dave Johnson
segments.text: How you doing? Dave Johnson.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Dave Johnson?

segments.speaker: Dave Johnson
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Hey. Get a little closer.

segments.speaker: Dave Johnson
segments.text: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So do you work here?

segments.speaker: Dave Johnson
segments.text: Yes, I do.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What do you do here?

segments.speaker: Dave Johnson
segments.text: I work Sky Trail and do Paul Bunyan occasionally.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHS] You're blowing their cover here.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Dave Johnson
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So was that you today?

segments.speaker: Dave Johnson
segments.text: Yeah, that was me. It was hot up there. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Your face is totally flushed.

segments.speaker: Dave Johnson
segments.text: Yeah, yeah. It's about 95 up there.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: His face really was bright red, though it took me a minute to realize what he meant when he said "up there." I had assumed that whoever was the voice of Paul Bunyan was looking out a window from the gift shop, which is right across the way. Or maybe they were watching a video monitor somewhere and talking into a mic, but no.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: John and Kylan, in a stunning reversal in their media strategy, I have to say, walked me around to see the back of Paul Bunyan's right shoe. And there's a little door there and they opened it up.

segments.speaker: Kylan
segments.text: We now see a ladder and a bunch of pipes and wires heading up.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I stick my head in and look up. It's dark and narrow. Kylan and Hannah offer to take me up, and I climb in first and it was stuffy and hot and claustrophobic. It felt very easy to fall.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So we just keep going up?

segments.speaker: Kylan
segments.text: Yep.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We climb this one ladder for what seems like a really long time and then switch to another ladder and then hoist ourselves through an opening.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Holy [BLEEP]!

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's like a little space capsule in here.

segments.speaker: Hannah
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Kylan
segments.text: It's about an eight to 10 foot oval.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We're inside Paul's torso. It's lit by a single bare light bulb on a wire that looks like if you touched the wire, you would die. You see outside through Paul's chest hair.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The walls are covered in decaying soundproofing tiles and torn installation. There's a dingy old sink that the guys pee into on their shifts, and old pressure gauges from 1962 measuring the hydraulics, four levers to make Paul's eye wink or head turn.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is amazing! This is really like a magical place, I have to say.

segments.speaker: Kylan
segments.text: The coolest things, I think, are these old, old hydraulics that control everything. See, you can feel this whole place shake.

segments.speaker: Kylan
segments.text: [RUMBLING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That's the hand?

segments.speaker: Kylan
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Hannah
segments.text: So do you think it's better now that you know? Or is it worse? Or is it the same?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I have to say this is better than not knowing. This is so cool in here, this room with these steel beams cutting through it and the crappy sink where people pee. This really is like going inside the Wizard of Oz's head.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Of course, right? Anybody with a secret identity probably feels this. They're supposed to keep it secret, but it must be so tempting to tell people the truth. It must be so hard to keep your mouth shut for spies and for superheroes, 'cause the truth is so insanely cool. How did Bruce Wayne not bring every woman he ever took on a date to see the Batcave?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Is this the microphone?

segments.speaker: Kylan
segments.text: I think so.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Is it live?

segments.speaker: Kylan
segments.text: You'd probably have a better shot.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, I would totally know how to work this. Yeah, this is totally technology that I know. One, two, three.

segments.speaker: Kylan
segments.text: That sounds live.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, it's on!

segments.speaker: Hannah
segments.text: Oops.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: From WBEZ Chicago and Public Radio International, it's This American Life. I'm Paul Bunyan. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act One, You Can't Handle the Truth. So I'm just guessing here, but I would think that people usually take on a secret identity only after careful consideration, only after thinking through all the angles, taking some time. Jon Ronson has this story of a guy who takes on a secret identity in haste without a lot of strategizing, without much long term thinking.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Sometimes the government stages crimes, like in the 1950s when the CIA was experimenting with LSD as a truth serum and they set up a fake brothel in New York City. The prostitutes would spike the unsuspecting johns' drinks with acid while CIA agents sat behind a one-way mirror to see if they would blurt out secrets. This really happened.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Just a few years ago, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives was telling gun shops to sell weapons to drug smugglers. The idea was to track the guns into the Mexican cartels. But the operation fell apart when they lost track of them and two turned up at the murder scene of a US Border Patrol agent.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: These kinds of covert operations happen quite a lot. Keep that in mind as you hear this story, which starts with a spate of attempted bank robberies in northern Virginia in June 2012.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: The man who carried them out was a terrible bank robber. And I don't mean he was terribly evil. I mean he was terrible at it. He'd stand there, demand money, suddenly look panicky, then run out the door.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: The entire spree lasted four days, five attempted robberies in all. He didn't make a penny.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: The police quickly caught up with him. He was a 21-year-old guy named Herson Torres. But things took a strange turn when they sat him down for questioning. Tom Schoenberg is a legal affairs reporter and he covered the story for Bloomberg Businessweek.

segments.speaker: Tom Schoenberg
segments.text: Initially, he didn't want to tell them anything. And he didn't tell them anything for a little bit. And they started showing him pictures of his relatives that they had assembled, and saying he could go to prison for 25 years.

segments.speaker: Tom Schoenberg
segments.text: By that point, he was crying. And he said, I want to tell you something, but you're not going to believe what I'm going to tell you.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: What Herson told them was unbelievable. But within hours of questioning Herson, the police began to think that his story might be true and that Herson was innocent.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: It all started, he said, a few days earlier. Herson had got home from a shift unloading trucks at Target when he saw that  he had a text message from an old high school friend, Carolina. Here's Tom Schoenberg again.

segments.speaker: Tom Schoenberg
segments.text: And the message says, hey, I've got a job for you. We're going to get paid $25,000. And he taps back, doing what? She responds, robbing banks.

segments.speaker: Tom Schoenberg
segments.text: And at first he thought it was a joke. She explains that it's all legitimate, that it's for the federal government. And he agreed to meet with her.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Three hours later when Herson was meeting Carolina in a nearby Dick's Sporting Goods parking lot, she was already on the phone to her government contact, a man named Theo who worked with the Defense Intelligence Agency, a part of the Department of Defense. She passed the phone over to Herson.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Theo started telling Herson that this was an operation using civilians to test the security of area banks. He'd vetted Herson, Theo said, so he knew all about a misdemeanor theft charge from when Herson was a teenager, the sort of charge that was sealed in juvenile records. And then Theo explained the job that Herson was being recruited into.

segments.speaker: Tom Schoenberg
segments.text: He calmly said the banks knew that this operation was happening, and he was going to tell them which bank to target. He explained how the whole operation would work out, that there would be no weapons involved, and that it was really a simple thing to go into these banks and see would they turn over money when someone comes in there and presents them with a note asking them to do so.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: OK, so when he said that the banks knew, that the bank head office knew, but the bank tellers didn't know and the local managers didn't know.

segments.speaker: Tom Schoenberg
segments.text: Exactly.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Tom Schoenberg
segments.text: Exactly.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Right. And so what would happen if Herson got into trouble in the bank, like if somebody tried to attack him or something in the bank or called the police?

segments.speaker: Tom Schoenberg
segments.text: Right. He was told-- and this is where his timing of going into these banks and out was very quick-- was that he was told do not stay in a bank for longer than five minutes. If anyone says they're going to call police, leave immediately.

segments.speaker: Tom Schoenberg
segments.text: If you see any armed security officers there, immediately leave. And if you get arrested, stay silent. We'll have you out within 24 hours.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: So how long after this phone call did the spate of robberies take place?

segments.speaker: Tom Schoenberg
segments.text: Immediately.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Well, like the next day?

segments.speaker: Tom Schoenberg
segments.text: The same day.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: The same day?

segments.speaker: Tom Schoenberg
segments.text: The same day.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Herson had plenty of reasons to go along with it. The government guy, Theo, was credible. He seemed to know all about Herson's past. He said he may be able to get Herson a full time government job.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Plus Herson was going to be well paid-- $25,000 if he managed to get money out of the banks, $2,500 if not.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: At the first bank, Herson handed them a note which read, "I need your help. I need money. My family is being held hostage and a bomb will go off at 4:30 if you don't help. Don't call the police or the FBI."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The teller asked Herson to wait for a few moments. Herson immediately ran out of the bank. Within minutes, the area was filled with police cars and a police helicopter. Theo was on Carolina's cell phone throughout it all, telling Herson which bank to go to next and to not worry.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Herson made four more attempts over the next two days, co-opting his cousin, his brother-in-law, and a friend. They were all as hopeless as Herson, running out of the banks before anyone could give them any money.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Plus they'd forgotten to bring a bag. So even if they had waited for the money, they'd have had to run out with it in their arms.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: At the last bank, the cousin just stood there while the others ran away. So the police questioned him. He gave them Herson's name and address, which is how the spree ended. So there was Herson at the police station, facing 25 years in prison and crying.

segments.speaker: Tom Schoenberg
segments.text: So when he finally tells police, look this is the story, he says, take a look at my phone. Look at my Facebook account. Look at my email. It's all there. He also told them, go to my car and in there, you'll find an immunity letter that Theo gave me.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Theo had emailed Herson a letter on Defense Intelligence Agency letterhead, describing the bank operation, titled "Operation Down Strike," an operation involving civilian volunteers who would be immune from civil and criminal action. It asks police that, upon receipt of the letter, to assist in the operation.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: The officer in charge, a veteran detective named John Vickery, was skeptical. But the letter was perplexing. And then, six hours after Herson was arrested, Detective Vickery got a call from a number he didn't recognize.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: It was Theo. He demanded to know what the police had done with Herson. He sounded authoritative and exasperated and explained that he was with the CIA.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Detective Vickery was truly confused. After all, this was Virginia, CIA country. Vickery did deal with CIA people from time to time. But it seemed such a strange covert operation.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Theo demanded a face-to-face meeting with the detective's superiors. Theo also called Washington area criminal defense lawyers, saying he was with the CIA and he needed to hire civilian counsel to defend Herson.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: The meeting place with the cops was set. It would be at the courthouse during Herson's arraignment hearing. Theo would be wearing an American flag pin on his black suit. The day came, but Theo never showed.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Eventually, the encryption on Theo's phone number was broken and police traced the phone to a man called Josh Brady, who lived in a ranch house 100 miles south of Washington, D.C. The police drove down there, and in an instant, three things became clear.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: The first was that Theo and Josh were the same person. The second was that Josh was not working for the CIA. He was 26 and living with his mother and grandmother. And the third was that Josh was totally convinced that he was working for them. Here's Tom.

segments.speaker: Tom Schoenberg
segments.text: I interviewed Josh in a jail in Virginia. And when I met with him, he told me pretty quickly that he was working with the CIA. And I would say he was firmly convinced at that time that they took a computer from his house that contained all the information to prove that this was legitimate.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Josh was initially charged with impersonating a government official and three counts of attempted bank robbery. But doctors found that Josh suffered from a variety of mental illnesses and disorders, so prosecutors dropped those charges and Josh was released into his mother's care and ordered to get mental health treatment. They declined to prosecute Herson and Carolina was never charged. In the end, no one was prosecuted for the attempted bank robberies.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: But here's something I found especially interesting about this story. During the court proceedings, a court appointed forensic psychologist had offered a second opinion about Josh Brady. He had diagnosed Josh with something really rare. It's a disorder that most people have never heard of. I'd never heard of it. It's called delusional disorder.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Herson Torres didn't want to talk to me for this story. Maybe he felt embarrassed about being taken in by Josh. But he shouldn't feel embarrassed, because the whole scheme, it was plausible. That's the amazing thing about delusional disorder, the delusions are plausible.

segments.speaker: Dr. Evan Nelson
segments.text: I mean, we all know that there are indeed folks who seem perfectly normal but turn out to be undercover agents. It doesn't violate the boundaries of reality.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: This is Dr. Evan Nelson, the court psychologist who diagnosed Josh Brady with delusional disorder. Dr. Nelson couldn't talk to me about Josh Brady's case, but he explained to me that delusional disorder is like a cousin to better known psychotic disorders like schizophrenia.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: The big difference is that people with schizophrenia have crazy delusions that nobody believes, like believing that the CIA is using telepathy to read your thoughts or believing that you're Jesus Christ. Whereas the delusions that come with delusional disorder, they could be true.

segments.speaker: Dr. Evan Nelson
segments.text: It's the difference between believing people are following you, which is entirely possible, and believing they're following you because they've inserted some sort of an x-ray machine in your body and they can covertly track you through a satellite that's orbiting Mars. That sort of violation of logic wouldn't be part of a delusional disorder.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Delusional disorder is defined as a rare disorder, but a lot of clinicians like Dr. Nelson believe that it has to be under-diagnosed. There have to be people out there who don't realize that they are living inside someone else's delusion-- like, for instance, my friend Emily, which isn't her real name. And this isn't her real voice either.

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: Well, my husband had it, so I lived with someone with delusional disorder.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: When you say your husband had it, does that mean he doesn't have it any more?

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: No. I mean, he probably still has it.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Emily asked to be disguised because she loves her husband and wants to protect his privacy. And so in a show about secret identities, this weird robot voice is her one.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Emily is the reason why I ever got to hear about Herson and Theo. She sent me a link to Tom's article. In the message she wrote, "Imagine being married to that. LOL."

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: By "that," Emily meant a marriage filled with the chaos of a plausible delusion. I said I couldn't imagine it. So Emily agreed to talk about it.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: When Emily first met her husband and when they first got married, everything was fine. He told her he'd been in a long term relationship before, but unfortunately it didn't work out.

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: He told me that his previous partner had been extremely unfaithful, unfaithful in the extreme. At the time, I just thought, oh, that's dreadful. You poor soul. I can't imagine what you've been through.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Emily says that for the first five years of their marriage, everything was normal. But then her husband had a bad turn professionally. It stressed him out. He worried about his job prospects and his finances, but mainly he worried about losing Emily. He started accusing her of having crushes and flirting with friends and coworkers.

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: I mean, it got to the point where I would be accused of sleeping with friends, coworkers, just random people. Like if I caught someone's eye and smiled at them on the street, it would be, how do you know that person? You had an affair with that guy, didn't you? That's why he was smiling at you.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: When would you have been having the affair? Because I presume that every night you were sleeping in the same bed as him.

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: Yeah. I mean, he would literally accuse me of getting up in the middle of night to go have secret assignations.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: While he slept?

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: While he was asleep, yeah.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: So at this point, did you think this is beyond regular jealousy?

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: Oh, absolutely.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: There are five main subtypes identified with delusional disorder. There's the persecutory type, believing a person or group of people are out to get you. There's the erotomanic type, believing a person-- usually a famous person-- is secretly in love with you and trying to be with you.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: There is somatic, thinking you've got a medical or health condition you don't have. Grandiosity, thinking you're special or have a high status, like, say, believing you work undercover for the CIA. And the last, as Emily discovered when she began desperately googling for some kind of explanation, delusional disorder jealousy subtype.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: The diagnosis made on the internet was later confirmed by a psychiatrist. Emily's husband's delusions weren't real, but his anger was. Inside his delusion, she was cheating on him all the time. It was a living hell for them both.

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: When someone's screaming at you for nine hours a day, your first response is maybe to get angry and scream back. But I would just watch him and it would almost be like the sound was turned down on a movie. It was just so sad to watch him be in such distress and be so separated from reality. It was just the saddest thing to watch and know that there's no way that you can help him.

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: You know, I used to invite people over for Sunday dinner. And I remember just him announcing to the table of diners that my wife has a lot of affairs. She's a right slut. And you know, I didn't know whether to laugh it off or what.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: What did the people around the table do?

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: I mean, this happens a lot. People maybe just thought he was joking. I mean, people just politely ignored it and moved on. And people didn't know whether it was just a bad joke or what.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Maybe some people believed him.

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: I had one chap that was convinced that I was the nymphomaniac that my husband had been boasting to everyone that I was. And so he came into the bedroom once when I was staying at a friend's house. And I just had to roll over and pretend to be asleep.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: What? Somebody came in and said I hear you enjoy having affairs with people. Would you care--

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: I mean, he didn't say anything, but he made a pass. So I just pretended to be asleep, because this is a person that I knew and I didn't want to be embarrassed about seeing the next day.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Wow! He must have been so crushed, because, you know, you're sleeping with everyone.

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: I know.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: And this is a crazy question, but when a delusion is as powerful as these delusions were, was there ever a moment, even though you knew you weren't having any affairs with anyone, was there ever a moment when you thought, my god, maybe I am having an affair?

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: I was honestly-- I mean, because my husband is a very rational human being. I mean, he was highly scientific. So when someone's that rational and that grounded in that level of reality, there was a point where I just thought, well, maybe I'm sleepwalking or maybe I've got a multiple personality disorder or something.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: Maybe I am the one that's mad.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: It's really difficult to treat delusional disorder. Dr. Nelson, the forensic psychologist, says logic doesn't work. They can't be talked out of it.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Anti-psychotic medications can work wonders for people with schizophrenia because they're good at tackling hallucinations. But for some reason, they're not so great on delusions. Dr. Nelson says medication can sort of lessen the delusions a bit, but they can't make them disappear. There is a best option, but it's a really frustrating one.

segments.speaker: Dr. Evan Nelson
segments.text: Gradually over time, you reach a sort of a detente, which is they're not willing to admit that their idea is a delusion, but they're willing to admit that acting on it isn't in their best interest. So I still suspect that my wife is cheating on me, but I know she says that it's not true. And I want to trust her. And our marriage is good, and every time I bring this up I make it worse. So maybe I'll just have to tolerate a little bit of infidelity in exchange for keeping this marriage.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Huh. So convince them that open marriages are the way forward.

segments.speaker: Dr. Evan Nelson
segments.text: [LAUGHS] Well, I don't know that that's necessarily an open marriage. I don't think they're consenting. But you're definitely talking about compromises.

segments.speaker: Dr. Evan Nelson
segments.text: Same thing with the persecutory type and the grandiose type. You may not get to the point where they agree that they weren't really acting as a special agent for the FBI, or where they agree that there isn't really a plot against them. But you might get them to the point where they agree that from a practical level, you've never been paid for your work from the FBI, so why bother to keep working for them?

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: The only way to move forward is for everyone to be submissive to the delusion. So someone like Emily never gets justice, never gets an apology for being taken all wrong. The delusion always wins. A few years ago Emily and her husband split up.

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: You know, people and places are triggers. So I actually became a trigger in my husband's life. So the only way for him to be healthy is to remove the triggers. So that's him moving to another new town and leaving me. And I'm sure that he'll find another woman in a new town, tell her the same story about the wife that was extremely unfaithful, and the cycle will begin again.

segments.speaker: Jon Ronson
segments.text: Incidentally, Josh Brady, the fake CIA agent who orchestrated the robberies, has been arrested again. A little under two months after he was released and remanded to psychiatric counseling, he was picked up again, this time charged with impersonating a Department of Homeland Security agent.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Jon Ronson. His latest book of nonfiction stories, Lost at Sea , comes out in paperback this week.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Coming up, a woman avenger takes to the streets with a gun and a mission of justice. Men fear her, nobody knows her name. That's one of the stories after the break in a minute for Chicago Public Radio and Public Radio International, when our program continues.

segments.text: Elna Baker, who's on our program now and then, has this cousin named Navey. And Navey has a secret identity that actually isn't so secret.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She's the school mascot, a tiger, at Gilbert High in Gilbert, Arizona. And she's one of those kids who's just completely transformative. Her second identity gives her power. Here's Elna to explain.

segments.speaker: Karl Baker
segments.text: I mean, I was fine with her being a dog, until she started crapping in our yard. I didn't think that was very funny. [LAUGHS] It is funny, though.

segments.text: That's Navey's dad, Karl. And at first I thought he was joking. But it turns out, one day he's looking out the window--

segments.speaker: Navey Baker
segments.text: And then I kicked my feet back to cover up the poop. [LAUGHS]

segments.text: And as she got older, Navey discovered a more socially acceptable way to do the same thing, when, in second grade, the elementary school mascot-- a husky dog-- stopped by her class for the first time. Navey's mind was blown, because here's this person who got to act like an animal all the time.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: She became obsessed with mascots. I know this because I babysat her for a whole week when she was 10. And while her siblings were outside in the yard playing, Navey was inside practicing mascot routines she'd found on YouTube.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: She'd be dressed up in this old tiger Halloween costume, a tiger because that's the mascot for the local high school. All of this started to worry Navey's dad, Karl. He was really hoping it would be a passing phase.

segments.speaker: Karl Baker
segments.text: I don't know if many parents wake up one morning and go, oh my gosh, I can't wait for my daughter to be a mascot.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And did you make fun of mascots when you were in high school or middle school?

segments.speaker: Karl Baker
segments.text: Now that's kind of an awkward question. Doesn't everybody? [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Karl Baker
segments.text: I remember being in junior high and really just trying to fit in. And I just didn't know if being this would be something that she would be accepted in. I mean, is this something that she gets branded as the odd girl who likes to dress up like a tiger?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: For years, her parents kept trying to get her interested in other things. More quote, unquote, "normal things" like ballet, Girl Scouts. But Navey had tiger tunnel vision. It all came to a head one Friday night at her brother's football game.

segments.speaker: Karl Baker
segments.text: Our older son was playing football in high school, and Navey's still in junior high. And I came home from work and I'm like, hey, Navey, we gotta hurry up. We gotta get to Justin's game.

segments.speaker: Navey Baker
segments.text: And I was like, I want to wear my mascot costume. Please let me wear it.

segments.speaker: Karl Baker
segments.text: I thought in my head, I says, I don't know if I feel comfortable with me taking my daughter to a football game dressed up like a mascot at a high school, because A, you don't go to high school there, and it's just kind of bizarre me walking into a football game with a tiger.

segments.speaker: Navey Baker
segments.text: And I was like, I don't want to go to the game if I can't wear my suit.

segments.speaker: Karl Baker
segments.text: And I says, you know what? Then stay home.

segments.speaker: Karl Baker
segments.text: So we're at the football game and she's texting my wife and just saying, hey, you don't love me. You don't support me as the mascot. You love the football player son, but you don't love the mascot daughter.

segments.speaker: Karl Baker
segments.text: And finally she texts me and she goes, listen, I still want to. Can I please come to the game? So we say, your grandma and grandpa haven't got here yet. We'll call them, they'll pick you up.

segments.speaker: Navey Baker
segments.text: And I took that as hey, I can wear the costume. So I get in the car, I'm wearing my costume. And my grandpa just said, did they say that you could wear it? I was like, yeah.

segments.speaker: Navey Baker
segments.text: And so I showed up, got out of the car. And everyone was like, oh my gosh. Hey, it's the tiger.

segments.speaker: Navey Baker
segments.text: And then I go and I look up and I was like, oh there's my parents. And I could tell they were not happy.

segments.speaker: Karl Baker
segments.text: And she looks at us, we look at her and those big giant mascot eyes. And she beelined it onto the field. And I thought, oh my gosh, what's going to happen?

segments.speaker: Karl Baker
segments.text: The sophomore cheerleaders didn't realize that she wasn't supposed to be there. And she's unbelievable. The crowd loves her. She's doing the wave, she's doing the cheer, she's leading the cheerleaders, football players are taking pictures with her. And no one has idea that it's a girl that's in eighth grade.

segments.speaker: Navey Baker
segments.text: They said everyone loved me. The crowd was cheering for me.

segments.speaker: Navey Baker
segments.text: Oh! I fricking love-- I can't even tell you! I feel like this is my calling.

segments.speaker: Karl Baker
segments.text: And that's when I finally said, listen, you have a gift. You should go and do  it 100%.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: This ended up being her big break. The high school athletic director was there and he came up to her after and said, look, if you want to do this again, just let us know. You're great.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And then he told her that she should try out to be the mascot when she got to high school. So since freshman year she's been the Gilbert High tiger. And all family pride aside, she is the best mascot I have ever seen. When she puts her costume on, which looks like a buff Tigger, Navey transforms.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: [CROWD CHEERING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She goes from being this awkward husky Mormon tomboy-- right, she's Mormon-- but she puts the costume on and then starts grinding like a male stripper. And it's hard not to think, are we allowed to do that? The kid has serious swagger.

segments.speaker: Karl Baker
segments.text: There's times where I sometimes forget it's my daughter. I don't picture her dancing because she doesn't walk around the house dancing. Immediately when she puts that outfit on, she knows all these moves. She can pretty much do any of the new fad dance moves.

segments.speaker: Karl Baker
segments.text: Beyonce's "Single Ladies," she can do that. She can do Psy. She can do Michael Jackson. The two don't really match up. It's bizarre.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: She's been on the news, she's in the paper. In town her parents are known as the Tiger's parents.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Some people come to games just to see her. The football team sucks. Sorry, Navey.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And she's gotten so much attention that recently the Suns Gorilla-- that's the mascot for the Phoenix Suns-- tweeted at her, "You're inspiring. That's no hashtag monkey business."

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Here she is at a dance-off against her rival, the Chandler Wolf. They're staring each other down across the 50 yard line.

segments.speaker: Man 2

segments.text: The wolf does the lawn mower. Navey, as the tiger, throws her head back and laughs, as if to say, that all you got? And then she busts out "Gangnam Style."

segments.text: [CROWD  CHEERING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She dances around him in a circle, shuffling and shimmying on the turns. And then she stops, face-to-face, and flicks her paws at him like, what are you going to do about it? And then, slowly, she backs away. And he shrugs, like I have nothing, and then bows to her, shakes her hand, and walks off the field.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, so that insanely confident person? Cut to the next day at school and she's just this super awkward teenager who doesn't want any attention drawn to her.

segments.speaker: Navey Baker
segments.text: Navey Baker is shy. During classes I just won't talk to kids around me. I just sit there and do my work, be quiet. I'm nervous to go to Taco Bell and order me a fricking burrito.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And is it weird to be two people?

segments.speaker: Navey Baker
segments.text: Yeah, it's like Superman. I mean, Superman, he's got glasses and a suit and tie. And then all of a sudden, he rips the suit and tie off and he's Superman. Except I put clothes on to become a tiger.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: This is how extreme it is. Navey's never been able to do a cartwheel. But then one practice with all the cheerleaders there, she thought, the tiger would do a cartwheel right now. And so she did one, just like that.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: She's done cartwheels in front of thousands since. But then Navey the person still can't do a cartwheel, which seemed impossible to me. So I asked her to try one out of costume.

segments.speaker: Navey Baker
segments.text: [LAUGHING] This is scary. I might hit something.

segments.text: All right, talk to me. Do you feel different all the sudden?

segments.speaker: Navey Baker
segments.text: Yeah, definitely. My heart's racing right now. My legs feel like running a mile.

segments.text: I just feel like let's go crazy. Let's go slide somewhere. Let's go slide on my belly onto the court.

segments.text: All right. Here we go, tiger. Let's see this cartwheel.

segments.text: Tiger is fist pumping the air. Tiger's bowing. All right, you want to take your hat off?

segments.text: Ah! Phew! I felt a lot better doing it in the costume than I did outside the costume.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Three, Blond Avenger. As we were putting together this week's radio show, we heard about a real life avenger with a secret identity in Mexico on the roads that run through Juarez, that incredibly violent city near the border, and to the maquilas, the factories on the border.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Writer Yuri Herrera lived on the border for years and spent a lot of time in Juarez. It's the inspiration for the setting of his first novel. And he tells the true story of what is going on with this right now. A warning that much of the story is not right for little kids and mentions sexual violence.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: The first murder happened at 7:45 AM on August 28th on bus route 4A. That morning, a woman hailed bus 718, climbed the steps, pulled a gun, and shot the driver. The driver jumped out of the bus trying to escape, but died on the sidewalk.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: The killer, witnesses said, was a middle-aged woman with dyed blond hair-- or maybe it was a wig-- wearing a cap, plaid shirt and jeans. Nobody saw how she escaped, or at least nobody would say.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: The second murder happened 24 hours later on the same route. A woman boarded the bus downtown and a few blocks later requested a stop. She walked towards the exit and motioned as if she were looking for the bus fare. But instead she drew her gun, spat words into the driver's ear, and shot him twice in the head, then fled the scene.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: One day later, a news website from El Paso called La Polaca, which specializes in covering the political gossip of Juarez, received an email.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: "You think that because we are women, we are weak. And that may be true. But only up to a point. Because even though we have nobody to defend us and we have to work long hours until late into the night to earn a living for our families, we can no longer be silent in the face of these acts that enrage us.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: We were victims of sexual violence from bus drivers working the maquila night shifts here in Juarez. And although a lot of people know about the things we've suffered, nobody defends us nor does anything to protect us.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: That's why I am an instrument that will take revenge for many women. For we are seen as weak, but in reality we are not. We are brave.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: And if we don't get respect, we will earn that respect with our own hands. We, the women of Juarez, are strong." The email was signed by someone calling herself Diana, Hunter of Bus Drivers.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: This year marks the 20th anniversary of the first disappearances of young women in Juarez, or at least when people started recording these disappearances and considering them as being related, after a 13-year-old girl was kidnapped and then found dead with signs of rape and strangulation. After that, the number of women who were killed just kept growing. It went from dozens of reported murders in a year to hundreds-- so many women, it was hard to count accurately.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: In 2010, the number peaked. At least 304 women were murdered that year. The circumstances of the crimes were eerily similar. One day, a girl would disappear on the way to work or on the way home. And if there was any news about her, it would be when her body was founded in the desert or an abandoned lot, often with traces of rape and torture. Sometimes they were found together in mass graves.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: Oscar Maynez, who worked some of these cases as a criminologist, explained to me the way the authorities became complicit in the murders. First, they deny the problem, he said. Then they played it down. And finally they blamed the victims' lifestyle and their families.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: The criminologist resigned, he says, after realizing his superiors were more interested in covering up investigations and tampering with evidence than in finding justice. So when I heard about the case of this woman, this Diana, who supposedly was trying to do something by herself, I wondered, after all these years without justice, if women in Juarez would look at Diana and say, it's about time. So I went down there to ask them.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: As you can imagine, most of the women I approached to get their opinions were reluctant to speak to a stranger about the woman who'd murdered bus drivers. "I know nothing about it," said a woman with a small child on the bus, only to fix her eyes on the back of the seat afterwards and not glance in my direction again. "I have no opinion about that," another one said before quickly entering a mall.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: But also one day I got this answer. "When I heard about what she did, I said, how great that someone's doing what many of us should have done."

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: This was Laura, 25 years old, pregnant with her second child. When I asked her if you were to run into Diana on the street, what would you say to her if you knew it was her? She said, "without a doubt, I would congratulate her."

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: There is a sense among the general population that buses are a bad place to be by yourself. Just this week, a bus driver was arrested for allegedly raping a girl on her way to school.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: About this Laura said, "I remember when I was in high school, I would hear a lot about it. My friends would say to me, if you're going on the route and no one's there, take a pen with you with the point facing outward, because you never know.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: That's been happening for years-- years. And it's the same for the ladies working in the maquilas."

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: There's no evidence that the bus drivers who were killed by the blond woman had actually committed a crime at all. But Laura didn't seem concerned about that. In a city where justice rarely brings results, maybe at some point you settle to get the justice available to you.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: Just a couple of weeks before the Diana the hunter case, Laura's younger sister, Maria Alejandra, 20 years old, suffered a home invasion. A man came in through her bedroom window in the night armed with a gun and tried to rape her.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: She recognized him. He lived in the neighborhood. After the man left her house, Maria Alejandra told her sister what happened and that she was going to report it to the police. Laura told her not to do that. What for? They knew how the police work.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: Laura told me, "I told her not to go, not to expose herself, because they would ask questions and check her. I think between the police, they've created a sort of code. So you basically are putting yourself out there to suffer one humiliation after another.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: "My father was with us. He wanted to go kill him. And my husband too, and me too.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: "I said, I'll kill him. I said I'll go and I'll kill him. Since we know who it is, we are going to go and do it with our own hands."

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: But despite Laura's pleading, Maria Alejandra, after talking to her friends, decided to go to the police anyway. And things went down exactly as Laura predicted. Even though the doctors had said that there was evidence of sexual assault, Maria Alejandra says the police questioned her as if she was making it all up.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: Why didn't she have bruises? What took her so long to report the intrusion? "I would have to almost be dying for them to investigate," Maria Alejandra says they told her.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: Laura was angry. Now the opportunity for revenge was gone. "I said to her, I told you. We should have done something before.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: "Because now if we took action, they would know who did it. Because that's how justice works here. The victims are the ones that are in jail."

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: In 2001, police did apprehend a bus driver, Victor Garcia Uribe. He was arrested with a colleague and accused of murdering eight women who were left in an old cotton field. He denied any involvement in the killings, but the police kept questioning him.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: Finally, after long hours of interrogation, he confessed to taking part in those murders and in the murders of three other women. Yes, he said, he enjoyed killing them. Yes, he said, they did it under the influence of marijuana, cocaine, and alcohol. Yes, they loved to rape them and kill them, and then they would throw them afterwards in an empty field.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: But two days later in court, Garcia Uribe did a complete 180. Again he denied that he was involved in the murders. He said he only confessed because officers had kidnapped him, taken him to a police academy, and tortured him until he did. He said they'd beaten him and burned him with cigarettes.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: Still, the judge convicted him and sentenced him to 50 years. Garcia Uribe was freed in 2005, after it was proven that the authorities had tortured him into confessing.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: "What makes me laugh," Laura told me, "is how the bus drivers are so scared. That's what really makes me laugh.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: I didn't see this myself, but Maria Alejandra says she's seen bus drivers who posted a sketch of Diana near their dashboards. And when a woman who looks like her tries to board the bus, they don't let her. She says they close the doors quickly now. And she's heard that some are carrying knives on them."

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: "You know what it is?" Laura said. "In this country, people don't have balls. That's why my dad has always said," Laura told me, "we don't have balls," he says. "Because if we had a little bit more balls, many things wouldn't be happening.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: We don't express what we think. We don't express how we feel. And we don't act in accordance with what we think. And that's our problem. That's what we are lacking."

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: So I asked her, but wait, weren't you on the verge of taking things into your own hands with your sister? "Yeah, but I'm not the kind of person who would do it. Sure, in the moment I reacted and I thought about it.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: But I would never do it. I would never try to kill anyone. It's not how I was brought up. I'm not like that."

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: While I was in Juarez, I spent more time riding the buses on route 4 than doing anything else. These buses, the Juarez public transportation buses, are old school buses imported from the US. They are noisy old buses, reasonably clean, but in a state of decay that everyone accepts.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: I rode in the back of the bus and in the front of the bus. I rode it at the time of the killings, in the morning, and late at night, when the last bus was about to finish the route. Sitting there, I wondered if the guy driving my bus was scared at all, nervous. I wonder if in moments on his route, he was thinking about Diana the Hunter, and the words she said to the second bus driver on the morning of August the 29th.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]. "You all think you are so tough." Right before shooting the driver twice in the head and running away.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: She hasn't been spotted since. And there's no proof that the email sent by Diana actually came from the woman who did the shootings.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: Whoever chose Diana's name chose well. Diana the Hunter is the goddess of women and childbirth, who, like many other Roman gods, acts out of basic human feelings, like rage and revenge.

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: There is, on one of Mexico City's most famous streets, a statue of Diana the Hunter. And there's a replica of it outside a restaurant in Juarez. She's muscular, strong, holding a bow with her arms stretched back, about to shoot. Maybe that image was in this one driver's mind on a bus I was riding when he opened the door and a woman came in and he said, "What? Are you Diana the Hunter?"

segments.speaker: Yuri Herrera
segments.text: "No, of course not," she replied. "What? Are you afraid of me now?" "Well yeah," he replied. "Shouldn't I be?"

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yuri Herrera. His novel Signs Leading Up to the End of the World is available in Spanish right now. It's going to come out in English next year.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We commissioned a piece of artwork of Diana the Hunter on the bus to go with his story from this artist named Alice Leora Briggs. She's been doing these incredible drawings of scenes from Juarez. You can see this piece of artwork at our website. We also have a link to her other drawings at thisamericanlife.org.
